characterList.description: A man with white hair and a floral tie. He sits at a desk in a news studio.
characterList.name: Interviewer

characterList.description: A man with white hair and a beard wearing a suit and a red tie. He is standing outdoors in a public square.
characterList.name: Jeremy Corbyn

content_metadata.description: An in-depth interview discussing the aftermath of the Brexit vote, focusing on economic and social implications.

qAndA.answer: 52% (This is visible on the screen throughout the interview).
qAndA.question: What percentage of votes did the "Leave" side win by?

qAndA.answer: He mentions a conversation Corbyn had with Andrew Marr, where Corbyn stated he was against an upper limit on immigration.
qAndA.question: What specific example does the Interviewer give to challenge Corbyn's stance on immigration?

qAndA.answer: He frowns and lowers his eyebrows, indicating he takes issue with the question.
qAndA.question: What facial expression does Corbyn make when the Interviewer asks him if Labour was "half-hearted" in its support for remaining in the EU?

qAndA.answer: He argues that it would lead to further cuts and austerity measures, impacting the poorest members of society.
qAndA.question: Why does Corbyn believe that an “emergency budget” would be detrimental?

qAndA.answer: He emphasizes the importance of maintaining effective trading relationships with the European Union.
qAndA.question: What does Corbyn say is "absolutely crucial" to the economic future of the UK after Brexit?

characterInteraction.description: The Interviewer challenges Jeremy Corbyn, sometimes interrupting him to pose follow-up questions. Corbyn remains calm and composed despite the challenging nature of some questions.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The interview discusses the significant political and socioeconomic impacts following Brexit, relevant to both UK and global audiences.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Shift from neutral to accusatory tone

narrativeProgression.description: The Interviewer questions Jeremy Corbyn about his support for remaining in the EU, focusing on his previous statement of being “7.5 out of 10” in favor.
Discussion of the reasons for the "Leave" vote, focusing on economic anxieties and immigration concerns.
Corbyn emphasizes the need for the Prime Minister to stabilize the economy and ensure trade deals with the EU.
Debate on whether Labour’s stance on immigration, specifically the lack of an upper limit, was a mistake.
Corbyn reiterates his belief that economic inequalities, wage undercutting, and exploitation of workers were key factors in the "Leave" vote.

scenes.thematicElements: The scene explores the fallout of the Brexit vote, particularly its economic and social implications.
scenes.title: Brexit Interview

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition from a woman speaking to the Interviewer
Split screen with the Interviewer in the studio on one side, and Jeremy Corbyn speaking outdoors on the other
On-screen text throughout, displaying news headlines and vote percentages by region

climax.description: Not applicable. The interview is more a discussion of the implications of Brexit rather than a traditional narrative with a climax.

content_metadata.title: Brexit Fallout Interview with Jeremy Corbyn

trimmingSuggestions.description: The scrolling vote percentages in the lower third of the screen could be trimmed at times, as they can distract from the interview itself.
Shortening the Interviewer's introductions to questions could make the scene more dynamic.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Mr Corbyn, thank you very much for coming here.
Good morning.
Good morning.
You famously said during this campaign,
you were seven and a half out of ten in favour of remaining.
Now your two and a half,
the two and a half side of your intellect has won,
and the seven and a half has been abandoned.
How do you see the future now?
Are you an enthusiastic Brexiter now?
Well, the British people have made that decision.
We must respect that result.
An article 50 has to be invoked now
so that we negotiate an exit from the European Union.
I think a lot of the message that's come back from this is
that many communities are fed up with cuts they've had,
fed up with economic dislocation
and feel very angry at the way they've been betrayed
and marginalized by successive governments
in very poor areas of the country.
And my point throughout the campaign was
that we had to have an alternative austerity.
We had to have greater resources going into areas
where there's been huge changes.
And I strongly called for the introduction
of a migrant impact fund
as well as proper funding of local authorities.
The results obviously are different across the country,
different between densely populated urban areas
and other parts of the country.
We now have to try and protect the working conditions
that we have in this country
and in the negotiations with the European Union.
Try to obviously ensure there are some trade opportunities
for Britain because clearly there are some very difficult days ahead.
The value of the pound is already fallen
and there will therefore be job consequences
as a result of this decision.
But we have to do everything we can
to try and protect jobs and working conditions in Britain.
If you want to do everything you can to protect jobs
and working conditions,
why do you want an abrupt article 50?
I.E. we've given two years to get out,
rather than what Daniel Hannan here a moment ago was suggesting,
which was take it easy.
Go and talk to the manure, think about it, discuss it here,
work out a strategy, and gently, gently,
you'll do much better than rushing headlong into article 50.
Obviously there has to be a strategy
but the whole point of the referendum was
that the public would be asked their opinion.
They've given their opinion
and I think it's up to Parliament
to now act upon that opinion.
But quite clearly, negotiations must take place.
There must be the best deal possible
in order to ensure strong industries in Britain remain strong
and strong industries that have big export markets
retain those export markets as far as we can.
But we are in some very difficult areas.
That's very obvious to everybody.
The accusation that Labour was half-hearted
and you in particular were rather half-hearted
with your seven and a half.
I don't know what you mean by that.
Seven and a half out of ten support for the EU.
Do you think you could have won this thing
if you had been ten out of ten for remaining in the EU?
The point I made throughout the campaign,
the point the Labour Party made throughout the campaign was
there were many people who were not particularly happy
with the European Union.
The point I was making was
that there were good things that had come from Europe
in working conditions and environmental protections,
but there were other issues that had not been addressed properly,
particularly economic inequalities in Britain.
And therefore, I said that my project was
that we should vote to remain in order to change
and reform the European Union
and put forward an economic strategy,
which isn't austerity, isn't punishing the poorest,
which is actually trying to ensure
that everyone gets a fair crack of the whip.
What about immigration, because you clearly laid out
your view of immigration, which there was no upper limit
to immigration into this country?
Many of the people who support you, I suspect,
but who voted to leave believe there should be an upper limit.
And you were very clear.
I remember seeing you say it to Andrew Ma, no upper limit.
What I was clear about was that the mistake.
What I was clear about was that within the single market
in the European Union, there has to be free movement
of people, and that we should also recognize
that more than a million British people
live in other parts of Europe,
and indeed, probably almost another million work
at various times in other parts of Europe.
And so if we remain in the single market,
then quite clearly, freement takes place.
But the very strong point I was making was
that there had to be an end to the undercutting of wages,
there had to be an end to the destroying
of working conditions in this country
by people being brought in by and screwed with employers.
The point I was making was that nobody should be exploitive,
and we should face that down
through the posting of workers directive.
If we no longer have an obligation to take anybody
who wishes to come here from the European Union to work,
what would your policy, Labour's policy be on immigration?
Well, at the moment, there is a controlled immigration
from the rest of the world.
There are often great difficulties over family reunion.
There are people that come in with particular skill sets
and particular jobs.
We will obviously have to develop an immigration policy,
which will be applying to Europe as well as to the rest of the world.
But I think we should also recognize that those
that have migrated this country have made an enormous contribution
to our society.
Indeed, there are 50,000 odd people
from other parts of Europe working in our national health service.
And so it is an important issue,
and we have to recognize the skill sets
that many have brought to this country
and given us a very good standard living.
But do you, that's interesting,
but do you accept that one of the reasons people voted to leave
was because they thought immigration was too high,
whether they were right or wrong about that in your view?
They did think that.
Many probably did, but there's also the question
of the impact of migration and the lack of government support
for areas that have been most effective.
So many of the poorest communities in Britain
have had the biggest cuts in central government expenditure
to support their local authorities.
And at the same time, it may refuse any special help
to deal with issues of school places and health places.
But you're often actually quite temporary issues,
but nevertheless, very important,
the central government recognizes those needs.
You make an elegant description about the problems that are there,
but do you think you just missed a trick here,
which was that people were much more worried about
actual numerical immigration than you gave them credit for?
You always said, oh, well, it would be all right
if there were more housing.
It would be all right if we stopped people being sent
on lower wages, all the posted workers directive
and all that sort of stuff.
Actually, it was the numbers people were worried about.
Well, I made those points because that is what I believe
to be the right way forward,
to end the exploitation of people whoever they are,
and ensure that our local authorities are properly funded
in all parts of this country.
This government has a strategy of systematically and quite deliberately
underfunding all local authorities
in the very poorest areas of this country
that face the greatest problems.
Mr Corbyn, what would you like to see the Prime Minister do now?
Do you think there should be...
Do you think there should be an election quite soon,
saying the autumn, because we've had a Prime Minister
who urged us to remain,
and the country decided to leave,
and it needs new policies?
The Prime Minister has some very urgent tasks ahead of him straight away,
one of which is to try to stabilize the value of the pound.
The other is to try and ensure the continuation
of long-term investment in manufacturing and other industries,
and then to begin the negotiations on the trade arrangements
that are with the European Union.
More than half our exports already go to the European Union.
Thousands of companies all over the country rely on trade
with the European Union.
That relationship with the European Union after X,
it is absolutely crucial to the economic future of this country.
I hope the Prime Minister is going to be concentrating very urgently on that.
What he does in the longer term is a matter of him
to decide what he wants to do and what the Conservative Party wants to do.
Our position is that we will oppose any urgent budget
that causes great cuts and further austerity on people.
We will support spending more resources in the areas
hardest hit by both the recession and changes,
and that we will try to get ready for a society
where there is a greater degree of fairness and equality
and obviously effective and efficient trading relationships
with the rest of the world.
In the meantime, in the national interest,
do you want Prime Minister and Chancellor of the Exchequer to stay in place?
I want them to decide now quickly what they are going to do
to try and stabilize the value of the pound,
and then they will no doubt be making a statement
to the House on Monday.
The important thing is to try to protect jobs at the present time.
Those jobs are partly dependent on the value of the currency
and obviously the export markets that are available.
Mr Corbyn, thank you very much for joining us.
Thank you very much.
